ann_37.text: Through this part, typical angina or non-anginal chest pain (about 22%) and atypical angina (about 28%) clearly lower a typical patient's predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms (about 59%).
Being a woman lowers it to about 6% (on the training data only).

More vessels coloured raise it steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same, to about 95% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher; higher cholesterol (about 39% at 193 mg/dL to about 81% at 308 mg/dL) and higher resting blood pressure (about 47% at 110 mm Hg to about 72% at 155 mm Hg) also raise it steadily (on the training data only).
A flat ST segment raises it to about 79% and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy to about 67% (on the training data only).
Through this part alone, a reversible defect on the thallium scan lowers it from about 59% to about 27% (on the training data only).

For two rare categories the model has little data on this: a fixed defect on the thallium scan (15 patients; about 16%) and a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; about 78%), both on the training data only.

ann_38.text: This part acts on 87 of 242 training patients (36%); 16 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 50-year-old man with atypical angina, a maximum heart rate of 171 beats per minute and a normal thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 11% to about 5% (on the training data only).

Through it, a higher maximum heart rate lowers a typical patient's predicted risk in an uneven way, from about 59% at 118 to about 32% at 175 beats per minute, and only once the heart rate rises above about 167 beats per minute (between 153 and 170 beats per minute for different patients; on the training data only).

ann_39.text: This part acts on 103 of 242 training patients (43%); 19 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 47-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain, a maximum heart rate of 163 beats per minute, a normal resting ECG and a normal thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 23% to about 3% (on the training data only).

Through it, older age raises a typical patient's predicted risk steadily up to about 59 years (between 57 and 64 years for different patients), then no further: from about 9% at 42 years to about 63% at 66 years, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower (on the training data only).
Older age clearly raises it here, in an uneven way, without a reversible thallium defect, but the other way with one (from about 9% to about 53%, against about 89% to about 31%).

Through it, a higher maximum heart rate lowers the predicted risk in an uneven way, mostly once it rises above about 167 beats per minute (between 153 and 170 beats per minute for different patients): from about 59% at 118 to about 32% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).

A higher maximum heart rate does nothing until about that point, then lowers the predicted risk steadily, and clearly more so without a reversible thallium defect (about 59% to about 32%, against about 67% to about 66% with one) and for patients aged 56 or younger (about 24% to about 10%, against about 63% to about 60% for older patients).

ann_40.text: This part acts on 108 of 242 training patients (45%), patients with a flat ST segment; 70 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 94% to about 98% (on the training data only).

Through it, a flat ST segment raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 74% (on the training data only), and a reversible defect on the thallium scan raises it only slightly, to about 63%.

Through it, older age raises it steadily up to about 59 years (between 57 and 64 years for different patients), then no further, from about 9% at 42 years to about 63% at 66 years, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower (on the training data only).

A higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way, mostly once it rises above about 167 beats per minute (between 153 and 170 beats per minute for different patients): from about 59% at 118 to about 32% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).
Higher cholesterol clearly raises it, in an uneven way, and even more so with an upsloping ST segment (from about 39% to about 81%, against about 81% to about 94% with a flat one).

ann_41.text: This part acts on 92 of 242 training patients (38%); 70 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 57-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, chest pain brought on by exercise, 1 vessel coloured, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it clearly raises the predicted risk from about 92% to above 99%.
Through it, a reversible defect on the thallium scan clearly raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 86%.
Having any chest pain symptoms clearly lowers it here, and even more so with a reversible defect (from about 67% to about 12%, against about 59% to about 22% with a normal scan).
Older age clearly raises it here, in an uneven way, without a reversible defect, but the other way with one (from about 9% to about 53%, against about 89% to about 31%).

A fixed thallium defect and chest pain type change that patient's predicted risk only slightly through this part, and age changes it only slightly, in an uneven way (on the training data only; the model has little data on fixed defects, 15 patients).

ann_42.text: This part acts on 116 of 242 training patients (48%), 79 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1 vessel coloured, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it clearly raises the predicted risk from about 92% to above 99%.
Through it, a reversible defect on the thallium scan clearly raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 88%.

More ST depression on exercise clearly raises it here, in an uneven way, and even more so with a reversible defect (from 0 to 2.8 mm, about 36% to about 99%, against about 59% to about 66% with a normal scan), flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher.
Typical angina clearly lowers it here, and even more so with a reversible defect (from about 67% to about 4%, against about 59% to about 11% with a normal scan).

Through this part, ST depression adds to the predicted risk only once it rises above about 1.4 mm, slowly at first, then faster (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 16% to about 51%; on the training data only).

A higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way, mostly once it rises above about 167 beats per minute (between 153 and 170 beats per minute for different patients; from about 59% to about 25% for the typical patient with a fold; on the training data only).

ann_43.text: This part acts on 84 of 242 training patients (35%); 46 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 64-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1 vessel coloured, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 99% to about 98% (on the training data only).
Through it, typical angina lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 40%, and older age (42 to 66 years) lowers it from about 59% to about 48% (on the training data only).

Age lowers the predicted risk through this part only once it rises above about 61 years (between 50 and 67 years for different patients; for the typical patient with a fold, from about 58% to about 42%; on the training data only).
A downsloping ST segment lowers it here from about 59% to about 27% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, 17 patients).
Higher cholesterol clearly raises it, in an uneven way, and even more so for patients aged 56 or younger (from about 13% to about 49%, against about 44% to about 71% for older patients).

ann_44.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 11%), non-anginal chest pain (about 22%) or atypical angina (about 28%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 59%).

Being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk to about 6%, more vessels coloured raise it steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same, to about 95% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher, and a flat ST segment raises it to about 88% (on the training data only).
Higher resting blood pressure raises it steadily, from about 47% at 110 mm Hg to about 72% at 155 mm Hg (on the training data only).

Higher cholesterol raises it in an uneven way, from about 39% at 193 mg/dL to about 81% at 308 mg/dL, and a higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way, from about 59% at 118 to about 32% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).
Signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG raise it to about 67% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise raises it slowly at first, then faster, for most patients, but for patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan it rises steadily: a typical patient goes from about 59% at 0 mm to about 66% at 2.8 mm, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher (on the training data only).
The model ignores exercise-induced angina and fasting blood sugar.

ann_37.original: Supported. linear_score is a 12-input logistic-regression term (SD 2.31 logit on train, AUC 0.850 alone) led by ca +1.11, sex:0 -0.91 (sex:1 +0.55, so male +), cp:4 +0.81, chol +0.80, thal:7 -0.64, slope:2 +0.48, thal:6 -0.48, trestbps +0.42. The negative thal:7/thal:6 weights are counter-directional on their own but are more than offset by the nonlinear paths (thal:7 adds +1.34 via young_reserve being shut and +2.87 via st_defect_hinge on average). Evidence: sensitivity = |weights| (train, n=242): ca 1.11, sex:0 0.91, cp:4 0.81, chol 0.80, thal:7 0.64, sex:1 0.55, slope:2 0.48, thal:6 0.48, trestbps 0.42, slope:3 0.23, restecg:2 0.18, cp:2 0.14. Train: SD 2.31 logit, AUC 0.850 alone; replacing it by its mean drops full AUC 0.959 -> 0.875.
ann_37.proposed: An additive part: chest pain symptoms and being a woman lower the predicted risk; more vessels, higher cholesterol, higher resting blood pressure, a flat ST segment and left ventricular hypertrophy raise it; a reversible thallium defect lowers it here, against its effect in other parts.

Three ReLU ramps on max heart rate: 5718 = ReLU(0.908 thalach - 0.10) (active 121/242) feeds young_reserve with weight 1.04; 7245 = ReLU(1.01 thalach - 1.53) (active 10) and 7595 = ReLU(0.994 thalach - 0.868) (active 49) read out -0.015 and -0.078: their joint logit contribution has SD 0.017 and is negligible (AUC unchanged at the mean). Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242): 5718 0.45, 7595 0.20, 7245 0.04 per unit thalach. Active counts 121/49/10. Readout of 7245+7595 SD 0.017 logit; setting it to its mean leaves train AUC 0.9594.

ann_39.original: Supported. 1718 = ReLU(-1.52 age - 1.14 thal:7 + 1.04 ReLU(0.91 thalach - 0.10) - 0.52) is a protective heart-rate-reserve gate: open for young patients without a reversible thallium defect who reach high max heart rate. Read out -1.13 (largest single nonlinear term after the hinge, SD 1.47 logit). Among non-thal:7 patients it is active for 60/60 youngest-tertile (mean 2.77, disease rate 0.10), 32/38 middle, 5/54 oldest; only 6/90 thal:7 patients. It drives the strong age effect for younger patients. 4256 = ReLU(-0.83*1718 - 1.06) is provably dead (pre-activation <= -1.06 since 1718 >= 0), so its +0.55 readout never contributes. Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242): age 0.64, thal:7 0.48, thalach_ramp 0.44 on 1718; 4256 all 0 (never active). Corr(1718, age) -0.78, corr(1718, thalach) +0.51. Disease rate 0.18 when 1718 active (n=103) vs 0.63 inactive. Setting the 1718 readout to its mean drops train AUC 0.959 -> 0.933.
ann_39.proposed: A part that acts on 103 patients and lowers their predicted risk; through it a higher maximum heart rate lowers the risk, most for younger patients without a reversible thallium defect, and older age raises it.

ann_40.original: Supported. 1476 = ReLU(1.18 slope:2 + 0.07 slope:1 - 0.37 chol + 0.08 young_reserve - 0.03) is a flat-ST-slope indicator: active for 108/110 slope:2 patients (mean 1.22, range 0-2.24) and 0 for all others; within slope:2 it falls with cholesterol (corr -0.99). Read out +0.55 to the logit (on top of slope:2's +0.48 linear weight) and +0.09 into hinge 1946. The young_reserve input (0.08) is a weak serial coupling, the reason young_reserve sits under this annotation. The negative chol term partly cancels chol's +0.80 linear weight in flat-slope patients (clinically unmotivated; not interpreted). Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242): slope:2 0.53, chol 0.16, young_reserve 0.04, slope:1 0.03. Active 108/110 slope:2, 0/132 others. Readout SD 0.37 logit; at its mean train AUC 0.959 -> 0.957.
ann_40.proposed: A part acting on patients with a flat ST segment that slightly raises their predicted risk; through it cholesterol raises the risk more with an upsloping ST segment.

ann_41.original: Supported. 3138 = ReLU(1.09 thal:7 + 0.11 thal:6 + 0.27 ReLU(0.995 thal:6 - 0.63) + 0.16 cp:4 - 0.31 age + 0.18) is a thallium-defect score: active for all 90 thal:7 patients (0.90-2.41, lower when older), all 15 thal:6 patients (0.12-1.25, boosted by the thal:6 flag 7354), and 2 others (<0.16). ST depression matters most with a reversible thallium defect, and older age raises the risk without such a defect but lowers it with one. It ignores exercise-induced angina and fasting blood sugar.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk of heart disease about 59%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk with typical angina (about 11%), non-anginal chest pain (about 22%) or atypical angina (about 28%).

Being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk to about 6%, while more vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raise it steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same, to about 95% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher, and a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 88% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise clearly raises the predicted risk, in an uneven way, and even more so if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect: going from 0 to 2.8 mm moves it from about 36% to about 99% with a reversible defect, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher, and from about 59% to about 66% with a normal scan (or the undecoded code 4).

Older age clearly raises the predicted risk, in an uneven way, if the thallium scan does not show a reversible defect, but the other way if it does: from about 9% to about 53% without one, and from about 89% to about 31% with one.

Higher resting blood pressure raises a typical patient's predicted risk steadily, from about 47% at 110 mm Hg to about 72% at 155 mm Hg, while a higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way, from about 59% at 118 to about 32% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).
The model ignores exercise-induced angina and fasting blood sugar.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

values.fbs: fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
